UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                     BEFORE THE
                       FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF THE
                MIDCONTINENT INDEPENDENT SYSTEM OPERATOR, INC.

          The Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”) respectfully submits1 this

Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer to the comments and protests filed in response to MISO’s

August 18, 2026 filing proposing revisions to its Open Access Transmission, Energy and

Operating Reserve Markets Tariff (“Tariff”) to establish Zero Generation Interconnection Service

(“ZG Interconnection Service” or “ZIGS”), a corresponding Zero Generation Interconnection

Agreement (“ZGIA”), and associated study, operational, market, and resource adequacy

requirements (“ZGIA Filing”).2

          The comments reflect substantial support for the fundamental design of the proposal in

MISO’s ZGIA Filing. The Organization of MISO States, Inc. (“OMS”) cautiously supports the

ZGIA Filing, but raises certain reliability and resource adequacy concerns of the states.3 The

MISO Transmission Owners (“MISO TOs”) support the ZGIA construct as an additional tool to

address large-load growth and provide greater consistency and structure for interconnection

requests designed to serve specific loads.4 The Solar Energy Industries Association (“SEIA”)

requirements minimize Transmission System impacts and protect other interconnection customers

from cost shifting.5 Google LLC (“Google”) describes the ZGIA as a “step in the right direction,”

while advocating for additional reforms beyond those proposed here.6 Advanced Energy United

(“United”) likewise supports the ZGIA subject to certain requested clarifications.7

         The remaining concerns do not demonstrate that MISO’s proposal is unjust or

unreasonable. The sole protest in this matter was filed by Community Organizations and Clean

Energy Advocates.8 Several comments and protests arise from a misunderstanding of the limited

nature of ZGIS or concern broader large-load issues MISO expressly reserved for subsequent

proposals. ZGIS does not provide ERIS, NRIS, Transmission Service, or a general right to inject

energy onto the Transmission System.9 Instead, ZGIS is a limited form of Interconnection Service

that allows an Interconnection Customer to connect its Generating Facility for the limited purpose

of delivering energy to designated ZG Associated Load, subject to the configuration, study, and

operational requirements established by the Tariff and ZGIA.10

         The Commission should therefore accept the ZGIA Filing without delaying its

implementation or requiring MISO to expand this proceeding to resolve distinct large-load,

transmission-service, or generator-interconnection issues.11             Accordingly, MISO respectfully

I.        MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

          Under Rule 213(a)(2) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, answers to

protests are generally not permitted.12 Nonetheless, the Commission waives this requirement

where an otherwise prohibited answer would clarify the issues under consideration, ensure

completeness of the record, or assist the Commission in its decision-making.13 MISO respectfully

submits that granting it leave to answer the comments and protests in this docket will assist the

Commission in its decision-making and facilitate the expeditious resolution of this matter by

clarifying the issues under consideration. Accordingly, Rule 213(a)(2) should be waived for good

cause shown.

II.       ANSWER

          A.       The ZGIA Is a Just and Reasonable Standalone Interconnection Service That
                   Need Not Await MISO’s Other Large-Load Reforms.

          While United supports acceptance of the ZGIA Tariff revisions, it asks the Commission to

delay implementation of ZGIS to permit further coordination with MISO’s forthcoming Load

Addition Resource Study (“LARS”) proposal and seeks additional explanation concerning how

the two processes will operate together.14 Google, from a different perspective, urges MISO to

 expand ZGIS beyond the same-substation configuration to encompass generation serving

electrically proximate load.15

         Neither request provides a basis to delay implementation of the ZGIA Filing. MISO

developed the ZGIA as a standalone proposal addressing the generator-interconnection service and

study framework applicable to generation serving ZG Associated Load connected at the same

substation and voltage level.16 ZG Associated Load does not have to be a Large Load. LARS, by

contrast, is intended to address distinct study issues associated with new generation and large load

that are electrically proximate by aligning the Transmission Service and Interconnection Service

evaluations in order to provide coordinated study results on an accelerated basis .17 LARS will not

grant ZG Interconnection Service and MISO has not proposed that participation in LARS is a

prerequisite to ZGIS.18 Neither the ZGIA nor LARS create a new Transmission Service product

for serving co-located or electrically proximate load.19

         MISO therefore does not need LARS to implement the ZGIA. They are two entirely

different, standalone processes with distinct use cases. The ZGIA establishes a discrete form of

Interconnection Service for generation serving load under the specific configuration and

the ZGIA independently while continuing to develop other complementary large-load reforms.21

         MISO’s decision to limit ZGIS to generation and load at the same substation and voltage

level likewise is deliberate.22 MISO considered both a narrower same-POI approach and a broader

approach encompassing electrically proximate generation and load, but determined that the

broader approach would introduce additional reliability and transmission-service questions,

including potential retail-wheeling considerations. Rather than delay implementation of ZGIS

while23 those broader issues are resolved, MISO proposed a configuration that can be studied and

implemented within the limited ZGIS framework.24

         The proposal therefore does not foreclose the broader reforms advocated by United or

Google. MISO expressly explained that the ZGIA addresses only some of the issues identified in

the Commission’s Show Cause Order and that other issues will be addressed through subsequent

proposals.25 The Commission should accept the discrete ZGIA Filing before it without awaiting

resolution of every related large-load issue.26

         B.       ZGIS Is a Limited Zero-Injection Service, and the Transient Tolerance
                  Window Does Not Confer an Injection Right.

            Clean Energy contends that the proposal does not adequately ensure that “zero means

zero,” emphasizing the possibility of injections during and outside the Transient Tolerance

Window and requesting additional penalties for unauthorized injections.27

           That argument conflates the scope of the Interconnection Service MISO proposes to

provide with the physical response of a Generating Facility following a transient event. ZGIS

provides no general right to inject energy onto the Transmission System and does not convey

Transmission Service.28 ZGIS permits the Generating Facility to operate only for the limited

purpose of delivering energy to its designated ZG Associated Load.29

           The Transient Tolerance Window does not alter those service limitations. The proposed

Tariff defines the Transient Tolerance Window as the period following a reduction or loss of ZG

Associated Load by the end of which the Generating Facility must reduce its injections to an

amount no greater than the Load of the ZG Associated Load.30 The Tariff limits that period to no

more than twenty seconds and subjects it to applicable Transmission Owner Local Planning

Criteria.31

           The Transient Tolerance Window reflects the physical reality that a Generating Facility

generally cannot respond instantaneously to a sudden reduction in associated load.32 Even where

communications and other equipment link the Generating Facility and ZG Associated Load, the

Generating Facility may require a finite period to reduce its production following an abrupt

transient response in the ZG Impact Assessment while requiring the Generating Facility to reduce

         An inadvertent transient flow therefore does not create an entitlement to inject energy onto

the Transmission System.35 Rather, MISO expressly studies injections occurring during the

Transient Tolerance Window by modeling the loss of ZG Associated Load and evaluating the

resulting stability and steady-state impacts.36 The ZG Impact Assessment must determine that no

Network Upgrades beyond those specifically allow for ZGIS are required to maintain reliability

under those conditions.37

         The proposal also imposes specific operational requirements designed to enforce the ZGIS

limitation. A ZG Resource must install communications and monitoring equipment enabling it to

monitor demand of the ZG Associated Load.38 It also must install equipment enabling the

Generating Facility to reduce its injections to a level that does not exceed demand of the ZG

Associated Load within the Transient Tolerance Window.39

         The Commission should not require MISO to characterize unauthorized ZGIS injections

as unreserved use. The existing unreserved-use provisions address Transmission Service and are

not the enforcement mechanism MISO proposes for ZGIS.42 MISO instead proposes to address

ZGIS compliance directly through the technical, operational, study, and contractual requirements

applicable to the ZG Resource.43 A potential for injection above an established interconnection

service limit is hardly unique to the ZGIA. Any Generating Facility, especially one with capacity

above its Interconnection Service level, has a similar potential. The Commission explored this

issue in Order No. 845 and found that existing GIA mechanisms were sufficient to address

unauthorized injections without establishing penalties.44 Should MISO determine in the future that

penalties have become necessary or appropriate for enforcing interconnection service limits, MISO

expects that it would explore potential penalty frameworks for application generally to all

interconnection agreements that have such a potential rather than singling out only some

generating facilities or service types for penalties. This docket, however, is not the appropriate

vehicle for considering such proposals.

         C.       MISO Appropriately Establishes Performance-Based System Protection
                  Requirements Rather Than Mandating a Single Technical Configuration.

          Clean Energy argues that the Tariff should specify a minimum configuration of System

Protection Facilities, require automatic corrective action, and prescribe specific testing and

inspection intervals.45

         MISO’s proposal instead establishes the required performance and permits the particular

equipment and configuration to be tailored to the ZG Resource, ZG Associated Load, Point of

Interconnection, and applicable Transmission Owner system.46 The ZG Resource must identify the

equipment it proposes to use to satisfy the injection limitations, and MISO must verify that the ZG

Resource can limit injections as proposed.47 MISO then documents the required equipment and

configuration in Appendix A of the ZGIA, making those requirements enforceable terms of

ZGIS.48

         This performance-based approach permits the technical solution to reflect the actual

configuration rather than assuming that a single prescribed technology is appropriate for every ZG

Resource.49 MISO and the applicable Transmission Owner remain involved in evaluating the

proposed configuration, and a project cannot proceed under ZGIS if the safeguards are insufficient

to satisfy the applicable study and operating requirements.50 By focusing on the required result,

this approach avoids limiting Interconnection Customers to certain types of equipment or

configurations that may be incomplete or rapidly obsolesce.

          Clean Energy’s testing concern similarly overlooks requirements already contained in

MISO’s pro forma ZGIA. Section 6.1 addresses pre-Commercial Operation Date testing and

modifications, including testing of control equipment used to limit injections at the Point of

Interconnection to the level of Interconnection Service specified in Appendix A and testing

necessary to ensure safe and reliable operation of the Interconnection Customer’s Interconnection

Facilities.51 Section 6.1 also provides for similar testing after initial operation where appropriate.52

Section 6.2 separately establishes post-Commercial Operation Date testing and modification

requirements.53

         The absence of a separate ZGIS-specific inspection interval therefore does not mean that

the control and protection equipment is exempt from testing.54 The MISO TOs likewise recognize

that the ZGIA provides a framework for addressing the control and protection systems necessary

to limit injections from generation serving associated load.55

         D.       The Twenty-Second Maximum Transient Tolerance Window Has a
                  Reasonable Engineering Basis.

         Clean Energy asks MISO to provide additional engineering support for the twenty-second

maximum Transient Tolerance Window and argues that the standards governing a shorter window

should appear in the Tariff rather than the Business Practices Manual.56

         The twenty-second maximum is tied to MISO’s existing planning methodology. MISO’s

dynamic simulations analyze transient response over a zero-to-twenty-second study period.57 The

 twenty-second maximum therefore permits MISO to evaluate the ZG Resource’s response during

the same period in which transient stability impacts are analyzed.58 If the study identifies a

reliability issue requiring a Network Upgrade that is incompatible with ZGIS, the project cannot

proceed through the ZGIA process.59

         The proposed Tariff itself establishes the controlling outer limit. The Transient Tolerance

Window “shall be no greater than 20 seconds” and is subject to applicable Transmission Owner

Local Planning Criteria.60 Thus, the Business Practices Manual cannot expand the permitted period

beyond twenty seconds.61 Rather, the BPM will identify the circumstances in which a shorter

interval applies.62 This is a reasonable balance between certainty and flexibility because there may

be circumstances where shorter Transient Tolerance Window is appropriate for reliability based

on situation-specific factors that are likely to be technical in nature. Requiring MISO to specify

these rules in in the Business Practices Manual ensures ZG Interconnection Customers are treated

consistently.

         The ZG Impact Assessment also includes the ZG Associated Load and simulates a scenario

in which that load trips offline.63 The resulting analyses evaluate injections occurring during the

Transient Tolerance Window and help validate the protection scheme necessary for the particular

ZGIA project.64

          The twenty-second limit therefore is not an authorization for every ZG Resource to inject

for twenty seconds.65 It is the maximum response interval within which a project must satisfy the

applicable study and operating requirements, subject to a shorter interval where Transmission

Owner Local Planning Criteria or the BPM so require.66

         E.      The ZGIA Provides Appropriate Operational Visibility and Verification.

         United requests clarification concerning MISO’s ongoing visibility into coordination

between the ZG Resource and ZG Associated Load after execution of the ZGIA and how

compliance with the Transient Tolerance Window and associated equipment requirements will be

monitored and verified.67

         The proposal includes multiple mechanisms that provide operational visibility and

facilitate verification. First, each ZG Resource must install communications and monitoring

equipment enabling it to monitor demand of the ZG Associated Load.68 The Resource must install

equipment enabling it to reduce injections to no greater than the demand of the ZG Associated

Load within the Transient Tolerance Window.69

         Second, an Interconnection Customer receiving ZGIS must install metering for the

Generating Facility that is separate from the metering used for the ZG Associated Load. 70 This

requirement allows the generation and associated load to be measured separately rather than netted

behind a common meter.71

           Third, a ZG Resource greater than 5 MW must register as a Generation Resource, Energy

Storage Resource, or Dispatchable Intermittent Resource, as applicable, and maintain the

registration required by the Tariff.72 MISO explained that the registration requirement provides

visibility of the ZG Resource and allows MISO to account for the gross amount of ZG Associated

Load.73

          Fourth, the equipment and configuration used to satisfy the injection limitations are

memorialized in Appendix A of the ZGIA and therefore remain enforceable requirements after the

initial study is complete.74 Changes to the studied configuration that could affect the impacts of

ZGIS are subject to MISO’s applicable modification rules.75

          Taken together, the communication, monitoring, metering, registration, testing, and

contractual requirements provide continuing mechanisms for observing and enforcing the

operational limitations applicable to ZGIS.76

          F.      MISO’s Study and Model-Reconciliation Processes Protect Existing DPP
                  Customers and Address the Asserted Cost-Shifting Concerns.

DPP, and MTEP study processes. Clean Energy contends that differences in study timing may

shift Network Upgrade costs to load and argues that a ZG Resource could use ZGIS as a pathway

to later obtain ERIS or NRIS.77 United requests additional clarification concerning base-case

reconciliation and cost responsibility for constraints identified through MTEP.78

          MISO’s filing already explains how the ZGIA and DPP models interact. ZGIA studies do

not include Interconnection Requests remaining in the generator interconnection queue that do not

yet have a GIA.79 Before each ZGIA cycle, Interconnection Requests with GIAs approved since

creation of the prior base case are added to the ZGIA base case.80 Those projects are not, however,

inserted into an ongoing DPP study.81

         Once a DPP cycle begins, its base case generally is not updated to add subsequently

approved ZGIA projects, except for ordinary changes resulting from withdrawals or generator

retirements.82 MISO designed that sequencing to ensure that transmission capacity available to

DPP projects is not taken away by ZGIA projects approved outside the DPP cycle.83 ZGIA projects

likewise do not use available transmission capacity reflected in the DPP and ERAS studies.84

         After the DPP cycle concludes, completed DPP, ZGIA, and EPR projects are incorporated

into a new MTEP base case.85 Any resulting reconciliation issues are addressed through MTEP,

and the next DPP cycle uses the reconciled MTEP base case. 86 As MISO explained, this process

“insulates existing DPP projects from negative impacts or cost shifts due to the existence of the

ZGIA process.”87

concerns raised by Clean Energy. The amount of Interconnection Service awarded to a ZG

            Similarly, if a project already participating in the DPP elects instead to pursue ZGIS, it

relinquishes the broader ERIS or NRIS service that could be obtained through its DPP request and

receives the more limited ZGIS.96 A later request for ERIS or NRIS would proceed through the

applicable queue process rather than retaining priority based on the ZGIA.

            The same service limitation addresses Clean Energy’s concern regarding the commitment

of the ZG Associated Load. ZGIS is restricted to serving the ZG Associated Load identified in the

Interconnection Request and memorialized in the ZGIA.97 MISO requires documentation of the

relationship between the ZG Resource and ZG Associated Load specifically because the ZG

Resource may serve only that designated load and to prevent speculative Interconnection

Requests.98

            If the ZG Associated Load does not materialize or ceases to exist, the ZG Resource does

not thereby acquire ERIS, NRIS, or a general right to inject onto the Transmission System.99 To

obtain broader Interconnection Service, the Generating Facility must proceed through the

applicable generator-interconnection process.100 It may not inject onto the Transmission System

until granted a right to do so by such process.

           Clean Energy contends that MISO’s proposal does not adequately address transparency

because the Tariff does not expressly require publication of ZGIA study reports, affected-system

results, required or deferred Network Upgrades, or associated Network Upgrade costs.101 This

objection is unfounded. These requirements are not currently imposed on Interconnection Requests

seeking Interconnection Service through other processes, such as the DPP and it is not necessary

to add such new requirements for ZGIAs independently from any large load transparency reforms.

MISO does not propose to reduce any generally applicable transparency requirements currently

established in the GIP for Interconnection Requests seeking ZGIS.

          ZGIA Interconnection Requests remain subject to MISO’s existing affected-system

coordination procedures and screening criteria, subject to the specific timing modifications

applicable to ZGIA requests.102 MISO must provide the information necessary for an Affected

System to study a ZG Interconnection Request prior to the applicable ZG Impact Assessment and

provide any affected-system analysis received to the ZG Interconnection Customer.103

          More fundamentally, Clean Energy’s concern regarding undisclosed or “deferred”

                  ZGIA.

recovery, prevent MISO’s regional processes from becoming prerequisites to state authorization

of retail service except as necessary to provide jurisdictional transmission service, and preserve

sufficient information for state regulators to perform their statutory responsibilities.125

Interconnection Service expressly states that ZGIS does not provide a right to serve, or a right to

Transmission Service to serve, ZG Associated Load or a retail customer except as permitted by

applicable state law.126
